corrections.source_says: The first author's name is Erdem Doğukan Yılmaz; the form drops the breve in Doğukan.
corrections.locator: p. 1, author byline (visually checked); repository citation_author metadata, https://alexandria.unisg.ch/handle/20.500.14171/135864

corrections.source_says: The survey received 37 initial responses and excluded 4 respondents who failed an attention check, leaving 33 analyzed. The recorded n_analyzed = 33 is correct, but the exclusions field should describe this filtering; 37 is a response count, not a randomized count.
corrections.quote: After filtering out 4 respondents who failed this check, our final sample consists of 33 developers.

corrections.source_says: The combined contrast contains different results across variants: original-text LSI shows no clear difference (0.0070, SE 0.0042, p = 0.1108), whereas neutralized-text LSI shows increased similarity (0.0069, SE 0.0032, p = 0.0416), meaning lower novelty. Use mixed for the combined entry, or separate the variants as no_clear_difference and treatment_lower on the novelty scale; an unqualified no_clear_difference does not describe both.
corrections.quote: In fact, in one of our specifications (column (3)), we even find some evidence that products become more similar to previous products.
corrections.locator: pp. 25-26, Table 6, columns (2)-(3), and Section 5.5; codebook Section 7 (reverse similarity for novelty)

corrections.source_says: All five contrasts have regression coefficients and standard errors, so each list should include regression_coefficient_se. The tables also provide p-values; SEs are clustered by category-treatment pair for Tables 2, 4 and 6, and by add-on-treatment pair for Table 5.
corrections.quote: Standard errors are robust to heteroskedasticity, clustered at the category-treatment group pair level and reported in parentheses. p-Values are reported in brackets.
corrections.locator: p. 19, Table 2; p. 23, Table 4; p. 24, Table 5; p. 25, Table 6, estimates and table notes

corrections.source_says: Replace the unresolved alternatives with mixed for all five outcomes: the analyses include products or updates from before and after ChatGPT became available, including a prior-year control period. Availability is the exposure; actual use by individual developers is not established by these main comparisons.
corrections.quote: The treatment group covers the period from June 2022 to May 2023, which is centered around the introduction of ChatGPT in November 2022.
corrections.locator: pp. 15-16, Section 4.4, footnote 13 and Figure 1; Tables 2, 4-6

corrections.source_says: Set not_met. The main analysis uses the same calendar months in the prior year as its control, and the separate developer survey measures reported experiences; neither randomly assigns people to AI assistance.
corrections.quote: PD has no such group and instead uses the same calendar months from the prior year as the control.
corrections.locator: pp. 15-18, Sections 4.4-4.5; pp. 43-44, Appendix D survey methods

corrections.source_says: Replace the unresolved alternatives with unclear at paper level, explaining that S1 does not report a distinct-person analysis count (retain null) and S2 has 33 analyzed people, so S2 is not_met. The 360 category-month observations and 41,880 add-on-month observations cannot establish the 50-person criterion. The survey is not a small randomized experiment.
corrections.quote: After filtering out 4 respondents who failed this check, our final sample consists of 33 developers.
corrections.locator: p. 14, Section 4.3; p. 17, footnote 19; p. 44, Appendix D.1

corrections.source_says: Set met for the observational corpus: novelty is assessed from the similarity of descriptions of actual add-on outputs to earlier add-ons. The developer survey itself has self-reports rather than scored creative output. This does not change core = no because random assignment is absent.
corrections.quote: To analyze whether new add-ons are novel (i.e., different from add-ons that were previously introduced to the market), we use the textual similarity of descriptions of newly introduced add-ons.
corrections.locator: pp. 25-26, Section 5.5 and Table 6; pp. 43-50, Appendix D

confirmed: Source independently read: the 50-page Strategic Management Journal version of record, DOI 10.1002/smj.70118, retrieved in memory from https://alexandria.unisg.ch/bitstreams/24ad1cd9-9fe8-4c7e-8d12-0fb137740e3e/download. All pages, including Appendices A-D, were read. The special-issue designation, received/revised/accepted dates, CC BY license, and 2026;1-50 pagination match p. 1; online publication on 2026-08-25 is confirmed by the repository citation_publication_date metadata.

The separate online Supporting Information is referenced on p. 35 and is not included in this PDF or independently read here; the form discloses the same limitation. Its descriptions of S1-S15 are consistent with the main article's references (pp. 13-18 and 25-27). No markdown conversion or PDF is listed as available in the local retrieval record.

S1 design_class = observational, eligibility.context_class = observational, and core = no are supported. The comparison uses June 2022-May 2023 against June 2021-May 2022, with June-October as pre and November-May as post; November 2022 is included in post despite the November 30 launch (pp. 15-18, Sections 4.4-4.5, footnote 13, Figure 1). No randomized people study is reported in the article or its included appendices.

Counts refer to products or panel observations: initial corpus 31,265 add-ons (p. 13, Section 4.2); update sample 1,745 add-ons and 41,880 observations (p. 14, Section 4.3); category panel 15 categories x 12 months x 2 periods = 360 observations, 180 per period (p. 17, footnote 19). A count of distinct people analyzed in S1 is not given, so its people counts remain null.

S2 is a survey of 33 analyzed developers, with no randomized assignment or scored creative output; it is below 50 people but is not a randomized experiment. Recruitment was through Upwork and required a Firefox add-on published before widespread GAI availability (pp. 43-44, Appendix D and D.1).

S1-O1 reported values match Table 6, columns (2)-(3): 0.0070 (SE 0.0042), p = 0.1108, constant 0.1514; neutralized text 0.0069 (SE 0.0032), p = 0.0416, constant 0.1989; 360 observations in each OLS model (p. 25). Section 5.5 confirms that higher similarity means less novelty (pp. 25-26).
S1-O2 reported values match Table 6, column (1): category count 0.0568 (SE 0.0239), p = 0.0241, constant 1.3700, 360 observations; the prose gives beta = 0.057, p = .0241 (p. 25, Section 5.5).

S1-O3 reported values match Table 2: OLS 7.3657 (SE 2.0216), p = 0.0010; log-OLS 0.2950 (SE 0.0727), p = 0.0003; Poisson 0.2476 (SE 0.0524), printed p = 0.0000; 360 observations in each model (p. 19). The reported 34.4% log-OLS increase is printed in Section 5.1 (p. 18).

S1-O4 reported values match Table 4: column (1), new-developer average rating, −0.1027 (SE 0.1536), p = 0.5090, 360 observations; column (5), rating within 30 days, −0.2641 (SE 0.1600), p = 0.1096, 329 observations (p. 23).

S1-O5 reported values match Table 5: OLS −0.0909 (SE 0.0215); log-OLS −0.0481 (SE 0.0095); Poisson −0.2263 (SE 0.0505); Logit −0.3233 (SE 0.0494); all printed p-values 0.0000; 41,880 observations for the first three models and 41,700 for Logit (p. 24). The 20.3% decrease is printed in Section 5.3 (p. 22).

The one_line_finding accurately reproduces the reported 34.4% increase in introductions, category-count increase, absence of reduced similarity, and 20.3% decrease in updates (pp. 18-19, 22, 24-26). This is original empirical research rather than a synthesis, so no pooled estimates or synthesis study counts apply (Sections 4-5).
summary: The observational classification, analyzed sample counts, reported estimates, and one-line finding are supported by the published PDF, which contains no randomized people study. Corrections concern omitted survey exclusions, the author's name, incomplete eligibility and outcome coding, and the differing novelty results across text variants.
